# The Hateful Immortals: A Documentary History of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage (1847–2024)

**Dr. Amelia Thornton, Ph.D.**
*Hargrove Chair of Applied Historical Studies, Reed College*
*Originally delivered as the Barker Memorial Lecture, November 2024*

---

## I. Preliminary Remarks and Scope of Inquiry

My name is Amelia Thornton. I hold the Hargrove Chair of Applied Historical Studies at Reed College, where I have taught for fourteen years. My previous publications include *Empowered Labor: Superability and the American Working Class, 1880–1945* (Harvard University Press, 2016) and *The Registry Problem: Federal Documentation of Enhanced Individuals in the Progressive Era* (Oxford, 2019). I mention these not out of vanity but because I want my audience to understand that I am, by temperament and training, a person who prefers primary sources to speculation, and evidence to narrative. I am not a storyteller. I am not, God willing, a romantic.

I say this because for eleven years I have been assembling, cataloguing, and cross-referencing the documentary record of a single American marriage, and I have come to believe that this project has required of me a kind of scholarly endurance I was not prepared to provide. I have read personal letters, court filings, therapists' session notes obtained through consent and subpoena, immigration records from six countries, a vineyard ledger, a hand-drawn chart of sleeping arrangements aboard a steamship, and approximately fourteen hundred pages of deposition testimony spread across nine separate legal proceedings, none of which resulted in a finalized divorce. I have, at various points, wanted to quit. I have, at one point—and I record this for the sake of full disclosure—thrown a folder of photocopied documents across my office and told a colleague that "these two people deserve each other and they deserve to suffer, and I will not be party to it any longer." I returned to the project the following morning.

The marriage in question is that of Margaret Greenbriar, born 1831 in Boston, Massachusetts, and James Chen, born 1828 in Boston, Massachusetts. They were wed on the fourteenth of June, 1849, at Trinity Episcopal Church. They are, at the time of this writing, still married. They reside in a duplex in Portland, Oregon—occupying separate units, sharing a wall and, depending on the season, a subscription to a single streaming service whose password they change to antagonize one another with a regularity that borders on the liturgical.

It is, to the best of my knowledge and the knowledge of every demographer I have consulted, the longest-running act of mutual devotion and mutual torment in recorded history.

I will prove this with evidence.

Let us begin with a daguerreotype.

The image, held in the Thornton Collection at Reed College's Special Archives under catalogue number TC-1849-001, depicts a young couple in formal Victorian dress.¹ The woman is seated; the man stands behind her left shoulder, one hand resting on the chair back. Both are stiff-postured and unsmiling, which was customary for the exposure requirements of the period and should not be mistaken for emotional content. The image is unremarkable except in two respects. The first is that both subjects appear to be in their late teens or early twenties—a point to which I will return. The second is that someone, using a fine metal instrument, has scratched into the copper backing of the plate, in tiny and furious cursive:

*He knows what he did.*

No date accompanies the inscription. Metallurgical analysis conducted in 2018 was unable to establish when the scratching occurred, only that the tool used was consistent with a sewing needle or hatpin. I believe the inscription was made by Margaret Greenbriar Chen. I believe it was made considerably later than 1849. And I believe that when she scratched those words into the back of her own wedding portrait, she intended them to be found—not by James, who would not have needed the reminder, but by someone like me, centuries down the line, who would require a thesis statement.

A note on the world these two people inhabit, which is also the world you and I inhabit, in case any of my audience requires the context plainly stated: the phenomenon colloquially known as "empowerment"—the spontaneous manifestation of anomalous abilities during puberty—has been documented with increasing rigor since the early eighteenth century. Current epidemiological estimates suggest that roughly one in every three hundred individuals manifests some form of enhanced capability between the ages of twelve and nineteen. The abilities are wildly heterogeneous. They range from the trivial (a woman in Bremen who can change the color of cut flowers by holding them) to the catastrophic (the Kharkov Incident, 1986, which I will not discuss here). The mechanism remains poorly understood. The social, legal, and political consequences are extensively studied, exhaustively debated, and largely irrelevant to this particular project, except insofar as they determine why the Greenbriar-Chen marriage endures.

What matters for our purposes is this: Margaret Greenbriar manifested total eidetic recall—a flawless, permanent, and involuntary preservation of all sensory experience from the moment of onset forward. And James Chen manifested something considerably blunter.

James Chen cannot die.

I have spent eleven years gathering the evidence to support what I believe to be the central claim of this study, which is this: these two powers, housed in these two people, bound by a vow neither understood at the time of its making, have produced the most extensively documented and forensically analyzable love in human history. It is also, by virtually every metric available to the historian, an absolute catastrophe.

The record will show that they have earned both designations.

---

¹ The daguerreotype was donated to the collection by Margaret Greenbriar Chen herself, who mailed it to my office in 2019 with a note reading: "I understand you are writing about us. You will need this. I have enclosed a self-addressed stamped envelope in the event that you come to your senses and wish to return it." The envelope remains unused.

## II. Origins: Boston, 1847

The following account of Margaret Greenbriar's empowerment is drawn from two sources: her own testimony, delivered during a 2003 oral history interview conducted by the Empowered Persons Archive Project at Columbia University (transcript EPAP-2003-0447), and a brief autobiographical sketch she wrote in 1912 for a Buenos Aires literary magazine that subsequently folded before publication. The sketch was recovered from the magazine's editorial files in 2014. Both accounts are consistent in their details, which should surprise no one.

Margaret Greenbriar was sixteen years old and reading in bed—a novel by Mrs. Gaskell, she specifies, though she also specifies that it was not a particularly good one—when she became aware of a change. The best description is the one she provided to the Columbia interviewer, sixty-seven minutes into the session:

> I did not gain a new ability so much as lose an old limitation. It was as though the walls of my mind became glass—everything preserved, nothing permitted to fade. Every word of every book I had ever read was suddenly present to me, simultaneously, in its exact placement on the page. Every conversation. Every room. The precise weave of the curtains in my mother's parlor. The sound my father's boots made on the second stair, which creaked, versus the fourth, which did not. I could not then, and cannot now, un-know anything I have known. There is no blur. I want to be very clear about that. Other people describe their memories as softening, losing their edges, becoming impressionistic over time. This does not happen to me. The first thing I ever consciously memorized after the onset—a passage of Tennyson I was assigned the following week—is exactly as vivid and as textured as the conversation I had with your assistant eleven minutes ago about whether the recording equipment was functioning. There is no hierarchy. There is no mercy. It is all equally present, all the time.

The interviewer asked whether this was distressing. Margaret replied: "At sixteen I found it exhilarating. At a hundred and sixteen I found it very nearly unsurvivable. At a hundred and seventy-two I have arrived at a position of what I will generously call détente with the condition. Ask me again in fifty years."

I note here that her self-description, while articulate, omits a social consequence that the historical record makes plain: Margaret Greenbriar, at sixteen, became functionally impossible to be around. Letters from her mother—Eleanor Greenbriar, née Lowell—held at the Massachusetts Historical Society describe a daughter who "corrects every spoken word as though the world were a proof in need of setting" and who has "driven the housemaid to tears no fewer than three times this month by recounting, at perfect length, promises made and not fulfilled." A former school friend, writing years later in a privately circulated memoir, notes that "Meg became a kind of court stenographer to one's own inadequacy." Margaret, for her part, does not dispute these characterizations. In the 2003 interview, she states: "I was not cruel. I was accurate. These were, unfortunately, indistinguishable."

James Chen's story requires less reconstruction, in part because his ability is less psychologically complex and in part because he did not, for the first century and a half of his life, spend much time reflecting on it publicly.

James was born in 1828 to Chen Weiming, a Canton-born merchant who had established a modest tea-importing business on the Boston waterfront, and Fiona Macphail, a Scottish seamstress who had arrived in Massachusetts the previous year and who, according to one account, married Weiming after he offered to carry her trunk from the dock and proceeded to carry it, without resting, for eleven blocks.² James was their only surviving child. He was, by all accounts, an amiable and notably incurious young man—a characterization that Margaret herself would, in later decades, simultaneously contest and confirm, sometimes within the same sentence.

In the winter of 1847, James Chen, nineteen years old, fell through the ice on Jamaica Pond while attempting to retrieve a hat. He was submerged for approximately twenty minutes. Two witnesses—a lamplighter and a woman walking her dog—testified to the Boston Constabulary that they saw him go under, assumed he had drowned, and were preparing to mark the spot when he surfaced, broke through the remaining ice with his forearms, and climbed onto the bank. He was not injured. He was not cold. The hat was lost.

James appears not to have understood the significance of this event for several weeks. It was only after a subsequent incident—he was kicked in the chest by a horse on State Street and experienced no pain, no bruising, and no interruption to his errand—that he mentioned the matter to his father, who reportedly listened in silence, then said: "Do not tell anyone. They will want to test it."

This was prescient advice. James did not, in fact, widely disclose his condition until the 1920s. But he did mention it to one person, within hours of the horse incident, for reasons that the documentary record does not explain and that I believe fall under the heading of "the irrational compulsions of a nineteen-year-old boy who has just met a girl."

They met at a public lecture on phrenology, held at the Boston Athenaeum on the fourteenth of March, 1847. I have confirmed the date through the Athenaeum's program records and through Margaret's own testimony, in which she observes: "It was a Thursday. The lecturer was a Dr. Pennwick, who had no doctorate. He was five feet seven inches tall and favored his left leg. He was wrong about the parietal bone, wrong about the faculty of acquisitiveness, and wrong about twelve other things which I will enumerate if you wish, though I suspect you do not."

The lecture ended. Margaret, by her account, was standing near the door, "composing in my mind the letter of correction I intended to send to Dr. Pennwick and also to the Athenaeum's programming committee," when a young man she did not know approached her and asked whether she had enjoyed the lecture.

She told him she had not.

He asked why.

She told him why. At length. With citations. She quoted, from memory, three passages from George Combe's *The Constitution of Man* that contradicted the lecturer's central claims, then two passages from the lecturer's own previously published pamphlet that contradicted his current claims, and then, as a flourish she would later describe as "unnecessary but satisfying," she recited a paragraph from a French anatomical text she had read once, two years earlier, in a bookshop she had visited for eleven minutes.

James Chen listened to all of this. And then—according to Margaret, and this is the only point in either the 2003 interview or the 1912 sketch where her syntax falters even slightly—he laughed.

"Not at me," she clarifies in the interview. "That is the thing I must be precise about. He did not laugh *at* me. He laughed the way a person laughs when they are delighted. He said, 'You just did all of that from memory, didn't you?' And I said, 'Obviously.' And he laughed again. And he said—"

Here the transcript indicates a pause of nine seconds.

"He said, 'That's the most amazing thing I've ever seen.' And I thought: there is something wrong with this man. And I was correct. But at the time—at the time it was the first—"

Another pause, seven seconds.

"It was new. The reaction was new."

She does not say, in the interview, that he was the first person who had ever responded to her ability with pleasure rather than discomfort. She does not need to. The record—the letters from her mother, the school friend's memoir, the silence that precedes her careful non-statement—says it for her.

He told her about the ice. About the horse. He told her, an hour after meeting her, things his father had warned him never to tell anyone. And she remembered every word, because she would remember every word of every conversation for the rest of her life, and because these particular words—this first confession, this first unearned trust—would become, over the next 177 years, load-bearing.

---

² This detail comes from a family history written by James in 1931 and submitted as an appendix to an immigration filing in Shanghai. The document is notable for being one of the few pieces of extended prose James ever produced voluntarily. His relationship to the written word was, throughout his life, considerably more casual than Margaret's—a disparity she noted frequently, with a consistency that suggests it was not, in fact, a minor concern.

## III. The Wedding—Trinity Episcopal, June 14, 1849

The marriage certificate is held at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. It is unremarkable: standard Episcopal form, witnessed by two parties (Margaret's cousin, Harold Greenbriar, and a friend of James's identified only as "T. Sullivan"), signed in both hands. Margaret's signature is precise and angular. James's is large (disproportionately so for the space provided) and tilts upward toward the right edge of the line.

The church registry at Trinity Episcopal confirms the ceremony. The minister was the Reverend Charles Woodhouse, who performed 143 weddings between 1840 and 1867, and who is not otherwise relevant to this study.

A letter from Margaret's mother, dated June 16, 1849, and addressed to a sister in Philadelphia, describes the event with what I would characterize as controlled ambivalence:

> The wedding was accomplished Thursday with all the usual forms and no disruptions. Mr. Chen conducted himself with good grace and wore a suit that, while not of the first quality, was well-fitted and clean. His father attended. His mother wore tartan, which I thought a peculiar choice but which Margaret later informed me was entirely appropriate to the woman's heritage, a point on which I was corrected at some length. The reception was held at our home and was, I believe, a success, though Margaret tells me I misremember the sequence of toasts, which I suppose I must accept, given the circumstances. I give the marriage my qualified approval and my prayers. I am told Mr. Chen is in good health. He does appear remarkably so.

Eleanor Greenbriar's "qualified approval" has been the subject of some speculation in secondary literature. Warren, in his 2008 essay "Mixed-Heritage Marriages in Antebellum Boston," argues that the qualification reflects racial prejudice toward James's Chinese parentage, and I believe this is the most plausible reading, though Eleanor's letters are careful enough to deny the historian easy certainty.
